screens.prose: Spread as a quant question. Suppose each application has a 5% chance of an offer, and the chances are independent.
screens.question: What is the chance of no offer from 30 applications? Give two decimal places.

hints.text: No offer means every application fails.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Multiply the chance of failing, 0.95, thirty times.

byKey.comp: That is the chance of at least one offer. The question asks for none.
byKey.sum: You added 30 × 5% = 150% and called the risk zero. Chances of independent events multiply, not add.

explain.text: Each application fails with chance 0.95, so all thirty fail with chance $0.95^{30} \approx 0.2146$. With fifteen it is $0.95^{15} \approx 0.4633$. Doubling the list roughly halves the risk here.

screens.prose: Maya sends 30 applications at 5% each. She says: "Only a 21% chance of no offer, so I am safe."

screens.question: What is wrong with her reasoning?

options.text: A weak CV or slow arithmetic fails everywhere at once, so 21% is optimistic
$0.95^{30}$ is not about 0.21
options.why: You doubted the arithmetic. It is right; the assumption behind it is the problem.

options.text: The risk is zero, since 30 × 5% is 150%
options.why: You added the chances. They multiply, and they cannot pass 100%.

options.text: Nothing; the firms are different, so the chances are independent
options.why: You assumed independence because the firms differ. The same weakness travels with her to every firm.

hints.text: Every row rests on the same things.
Shared weaknesses make the failures move together, so the true chance of no offer is higher.

feedback.correct: The failures are linked, so the risk is higher than 21%.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask whether one weakness affects every application.

byKey.indep: You treated different firms as independent draws. The same CV and the same skills go to all of them, so the outcomes are linked.

explain.text: Every application uses the same CV and the same skills. If those are weak, they fail together, so the real chance of no offer is above 21%. Raise $p$ by preparation, not only $n$ by sending more.

screens.prose: We worked out both numbers from the same model: $n$ independent applications, each with chance $p$. $$P(\text{no offer}) = (1-p)^n, \qquad E[\text{offers}] = np$$ Both are optimistic when the applications share a weakness.
screens.question: What is the expected number of offers from 30 applications at 5%?

feedback.correct: 1.5 offers on average, against 0.75 from fifteen.

byKey.fifteen: That is fifteen applications. This is thirty.
byKey.pct: You wrote 150 as a percentage. Give the number of offers, 1.5.

explain.text: $E[\text{offers}] = np = 30 \times 0.05 = 1.5$; fifteen applications give $0.75$. An average of 1.5 still leaves about a 21% chance of none, under independence. With linked failures the chance of none is higher.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Say in one word what she has done.

explain.text: A status says what you have done, and a next action with a date says what comes next. Kept this way, the list tells you every morning what is due. You build your own dated list in homework 1.

ideas: Filter a target list by eligibility first, then fit (track, region, timing), then spread across firm types.
With $n$ independent applications at chance $p$: $P(\text{no offer}) = (1-p)^n$ and $E[\text{offers}] = np$.
Applications share your CV and skills, so failures are linked. Raise $p$ by preparing, not only $n$.

formula.name: Chance of no offer
formula.note: Only if independent; shared weaknesses make it larger.

summary.trap: Thirty applications at 5% is not a 21% risk if the same weakness sinks them all.

quiz.prose: Ten independent applications, each with a 10% chance of an offer.
quiz.question: What is the chance of no offer? Give two decimal places.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Raise 0.9 to the tenth power.

byKey.comp: That is at least one offer.

explain.text: All ten fail with chance $0.9^{10} \approx 0.3487$. As a check, $0.9^5 \approx 0.59$ and $0.59^2 \approx 0.35$.

quiz.question: Your thirty applications share one weak CV. Which change most lowers your chance of no offer?

options.text: Fix the CV and practise, raising the chance at every firm
Send thirty more with the same CV
options.why: You raised $n$, but the same weakness sinks the new ones too.

options.text: Wait for the deadlines to pass
options.why: Waiting changes nothing about the chance.

feedback.correct: Raise $p$ where the weakness is shared.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask what links the failures.

explain.text: A shared weakness links every application. Fixing it raises $p$ everywhere at once, which more copies of the same CV cannot do.
